_comment: Hand-written coursework, one lesson per unit, keyed by unit id from units.json. Deliberately not model-generated: a beginner's first contact with a language should be the same every time, correct, and free of quota. Step types: 'sounds' (pronunciation), 'words' (vocabulary, each spoken), 'grammar' (explained in English with examples and an optional table), 'check' (one question, graded on the device). Keep every explanation shorter than it wants to be.

a1.1-1.title: Hallo und Tschüss
a1.1-1.intro: Your first German. By the end of this lesson you can greet someone, say your name, say where you are from, and ask someone the same back. Nothing here assumes you have seen German before.

steps.title: Five sounds, then you can read almost anything
steps.body: German spelling is honest: a letter almost always sounds the same way. Five rules cover most of it, and you can come back to this page any time.
steps.note: So 'wie' is said 'vee', and 'Wien' is 'veen'. The two dots in ä, ö, ü change the vowel — you will pick them up by ear, and the tutor will say them for you as often as you like.

steps.title: Hello and goodbye
steps.body: German separates the time of day. Nobody will mind if you get it wrong, but these four will cover your whole day.

items.note: safe at any time, with anyone
the normal daytime greeting; there is no German 'good afternoon'
formal; in a shop or an office

steps.title: du and Sie — the one choice you make constantly
steps.body: German has two words for 'you'. 'du' is for friends, family, children and most colleagues. 'Sie' is for strangers, officials, shopkeepers, your landlord and anyone much older. Sie is always written with a capital S. Getting it wrong is a small thing — Germans will often invite you to switch with 'Wir können uns duzen' — but using Sie first is never rude.
steps.note: At work in Germany, software teams are usually du. The Ausländerbehörde is definitely Sie.

steps.title: ich bin — I am
steps.body: 'sein' means 'to be'. It is irregular in every language and German is no exception, so learn these as whole words rather than as a rule. These four cover nearly everything you need at the start.

steps.question: You meet your new neighbour. How do you say 'I am Ahmad'?
steps.why: 'ich' always goes with 'bin'. 'du bist' would be telling her that she is Ahmad.

steps.title: Saying who you are
steps.body: Two ways to give your name. 'Ich heiße' is the more German-sounding one, and it is what you will hear back.

items.note: German has no separate 'am learning' — one form does both

steps.title: Asking back: the W-questions
steps.body: German question words mostly start with W, and the verb comes straight after them. Learn the question and its answer together — that pairing is what makes a conversation possible.
steps.note: woher = where from, wo = where. One letter, and it is the difference between your country and your street.

steps.question: Someone asks 'Woher kommst du?'. What are they asking?
steps.why: woher = where from. 'Wo wohnst du?' would be where you live.

steps.title: Numbers 0 to 12
steps.body: You need these for times, prices and your phone number. Say them out loud — the tutor will ask you for them later.
steps.note: On the phone Germans often say 'zwo' instead of 'zwei', so it cannot be confused with 'drei'.

steps.title: The verb comes second. Always.
steps.body: This is the one rule that makes German sound German. In a normal statement the verb is the second thing in the sentence — not necessarily the second word, but the second block. Whatever you put first, the verb follows it immediately, and the subject moves behind the verb.

examples.note: put the place first and 'ich' moves behind the verb

steps.note: This will be your most common mistake for months, and the tutor will keep catching it. That is normal and it is not a sign you are bad at this.

steps.question: Which one is correct German?
steps.why: 'Heute' takes the first slot, so the verb 'arbeite' must come second and 'ich' goes after it.

steps.title: When you are stuck
steps.body: The most useful sentences in the language. Learn these before anything else and you can survive any conversation.

items.note: this one buys you enormous patience

a1.1-1.outro: That is everything you need to introduce yourself. Now go and use it: open Talk and pick 'Die neue Nachbarin'. You will get it wrong, and that is the entire point — the tutor collects your mistakes so the drills can target them.

a1.1-2.title: Zahlen, Zeit, Termine
a1.1-2.intro: Numbers, the clock and arranging a time. This is the unit that makes you useful in a standup and at a counter.

steps.title: Numbers 13 to 100
steps.body: Thirteen to nineteen are just the digit plus 'zehn'. The tens are the digit plus 'zig'.

steps.title: German says numbers backwards
steps.body: Above twenty, the small digit comes first, joined by 'und'. 21 is 'one-and-twenty'. It feels wrong for about a week and then it stops bothering you.
steps.note: This is why Germans often repeat phone numbers in pairs, and why you should ask for a number twice.

steps.question: What is 'vierundzwanzig'?
steps.why: vier (4) und zwanzig (20) — the small number is said first, so 24.

steps.title: haben — to have
steps.body: After 'sein', this is the verb you will use most. It is irregular too, so again: learn the forms as words.

examples.de: Wir haben ein Meeting um zehn.
examples.en: We have a meeting at ten.

steps.title: Yes/no questions: put the verb first
steps.body: To turn a statement into a question that expects yes or no, move the verb to the front. That is the whole rule — no extra word, no 'do' like in English.

steps.title: Telling the time
steps.body: Germans use 'halb' differently from English: halb drei is half *to* three, not half past. It is 2:30.

steps.question: A colleague says the call is 'um halb zehn'. When is it?
steps.why: halb zehn is halfway to ten, so 9:30. This one catches everybody at least once.

items.note: used for anything scheduled, including a doctor or a call

steps.title: Regular verbs: one ending per person
steps.body: Most German verbs are regular. Take the stem and add the ending. Once you have this, you have hundreds of verbs.

steps.question: How do you ask a colleague 'do you have time on Monday?'
options: Hast du am Montag Zeit haben?
steps.why: A yes/no question puts the verb first: Hast du …?

a1.1-2.outro: Now arrange a time out loud. Open Talk and pick the standup scenario — you will need 'um … Uhr' and 'Hast du Zeit?' within the first minute.
